fields.Question: The interviewer says "Design Twitter" and goes quiet. How do you run the next 45 minutes?
fields.Answer:
Drive with a fixed structure.

  • Requirements (5 min): functional (post, follow, home timeline), non functional (read heavy, timeline p99 under about 200 ms, eventual consistency fine), explicit out of scope.
  • Estimates (3 min): only the numbers that drive a decision, such as read and write QPS and storage per year.
  • Core entities and API (5 min): POST /tweets, GET /timeline?cursor=.
  • High level design (10 min): walk one write and one read end to end.
  • Deep dives (15 min): the 2 or 3 hard parts (fanout, celebrities, partitioning), with tradeoffs.
  • Wrap up: bottlenecks, failure modes, what changes at 10x.

Pitfalls: boxes before scope, 15 minutes of math, naming tech without a reason, never stating a tradeoff.
fields.Hint: Requirements, estimates, API, high level, deep dives.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: System Design in a Hurry (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/introduction)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: 100 million daily active users each post 10 times a day. What is the average write QPS?
fields.Choices:
About 12,000 per second
About 1,200 per second
About 120,000 per second
About 1,000,000 per second
fields.Correct: About 12,000 per second
fields.Explanation: 100M x 10 = 1 billion writes a day. A day has about 86,400 seconds (round to 100,000 for mental math), so about 11,600 per second, call it 12k average and roughly 2x to 3x that at peak. 1,200 drops a factor of 10, usually by dividing by 864,000. 120,000 is what you get by forgetting a zero in the seconds per day. 1,000,000 divides by 1,000 instead of 86,400.
fields.Hint: Seconds in a day is about 10^5.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A URL shortener stores 500 million new URLs per month, about 500 bytes per record, kept for 5 years. Roughly how much storage before replication?
fields.Choices:
About 1.5 TB
About 150 TB
About 15 PB
About 15 TB
fields.Correct: About 15 TB
fields.Explanation: 500M x 12 x 5 = 30 billion records. 30 billion x 500 bytes = 15 x 10^12 bytes = 15 TB. 1.5 TB and 150 TB are off by a factor of 10, the usual slip when counting zeros. 15 PB confuses 10^12 with 10^15. Mention replication (often 3x) separately.
fields.Hint: Records times bytes, then count the zeros.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A video edge serves 1,000 requests per second, each a 1 MB segment. What network egress does it need?
fields.Choices:
About 1 Gbps
About 800 Mbps
About 8 Gbps
About 80 Gbps
fields.Correct: About 8 Gbps
fields.Explanation: 1,000 x 1 MB = 1 GB/s, and network links are quoted in bits, so 1 GB/s is 8 Gbps. 1 Gbps is the bits versus bytes mistake. 800 Mbps drops a factor of 10 (100 MB/s times 8). 80 Gbps adds a factor of 10.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Using the classic latency numbers, which of these is slowest?
fields.Choices:
Reading 1 MB sequentially from memory
One network round trip from California to the Netherlands
Reading 1 MB sequentially from SSD
A round trip inside the same datacenter
fields.Correct: One network round trip from California to the Netherlands
fields.Explanation: A transatlantic round trip is about 150 ms, bounded by the speed of light. Reading 1 MB from memory is microseconds, 1 MB from SSD is about 1 ms or less, and a same datacenter round trip is about 0.5 ms. Candidates often overestimate disk and underestimate geography, which is why multi region writes are expensive.
fields.Source: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know (https://gist.github.com/jboner/2841832)

fields.Question: A service handles 2,000 requests per second with 50 ms average latency. How many requests are in flight on average?
fields.Explanation: Little's law: L = lambda x W = 2,000/s x 0.05 s = 100. This sizes thread pools and connection pools. 40 is 2,000 divided by 50 (treating ms as a count). 2,000 confuses throughput with concurrency. 40,000 divides by 0.05 instead of multiplying.
fields.Source: A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = lambda W (https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383)

fields.Question: You are interviewing at senior level. The high level design is done with 20 minutes left. What does the interviewer most want next?
fields.Choices:
Add more components to show breadth across the whole system
Redo the capacity estimates with more precision
Write the full SQL schema for every table
Pick the 2 or 3 hardest parts and go deep on tradeoffs and failure modes
fields.Correct: Pick the 2 or 3 hardest parts and go deep on tradeoffs and failure modes
fields.Explanation: Senior loops are graded on depth in a few areas: the bottleneck, contention point or failure mode, with the alternatives you rejected and why. More boxes is mid level breadth. Precise estimates rarely change a decision once the order of magnitude is known. A full schema burns time on detail that does not show judgement.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: System Design in a Hurry (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/introduction)
Hello Interview: Design Ticketmaster (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/ticketmaster)

fields.Question: A read heavy profile service uses cache aside with Redis. On a cache miss, what does the service do?
fields.Choices:
Return a miss to the client and let Redis load the value in the background
Ask Redis to fetch the row from the database itself
Read the database, store the value in Redis with a TTL, return it
Write the row back to the database so the cache sees it
fields.Correct: Read the database, store the value in Redis with a TTL, return it
fields.Explanation: In cache aside the application owns the cache: on miss it reads the source of truth, populates the cache with a TTL and returns. Redis does not load from your database; that would be read through, which needs a cache layer that knows the database. Returning a miss to the client pushes the problem to callers. Rewriting the row changes nothing in the cache.
fields.Hint: The application, not the cache, does the work.
fields.Source: Cache-Aside pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)

fields.Question: Cache aside, many concurrent writers, staleness must be short. What does the write path do?
fields.Choices:
Update the cache, then the database
Update the database, then delete the cache key
Update the database, then set the cache to the new value
Update the database and wait for the TTL to expire
fields.Correct: Update the database, then delete the cache key
fields.Explanation: Deleting after the database commit means the next read reloads fresh data, and deletes are idempotent so racing writers cannot leave an older value behind (a slow reader refilling an old value can still race a delete, which memcache leases close). Writing the cache first leaves a value that was never committed if the database write fails. Setting the new value races: two writers can commit A then B but set the cache B then A, leaving A forever. Waiting for TTL means stale reads for the whole TTL. Facebook's memcache uses delete on write for this reason.
fields.Hint: Which operation is safe to repeat in any order?
fields.Source:
Cache-Aside pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/cache-aside)
Scaling Memcache at Facebook (https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala)

fields.Question: A key read 10,000 times per second expires, and all those requests miss at once and hit the database. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Let one request rebuild the key while the others wait or get the stale value
Lower the TTL so the key refreshes more often
Add database read replicas to absorb the misses
Give the Redis node more memory
fields.Correct: Let one request rebuild the key while the others wait or get the stale value
fields.Explanation: This is a cache stampede. Request coalescing (a short lock or lease on refill, as in Facebook memcache leases) or probabilistic early refresh means only one rebuild hits the database. A lower TTL makes stampedes more frequent. Replicas only raise the ceiling and still take a burst of identical queries. Memory has nothing to do with expiry.
fields.Hint: Only one request needs to do the rebuild.
fields.Source: Scaling Memcache at Facebook (https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala)

fields.Question: One key gets 500,000 reads per second, more than a single Redis shard can serve. The rest of the cluster is idle. What helps?
fields.Choices:
Add more shards to the cluster
Switch the cluster to consistent hashing
Change the cache to write through
Replicate that key: a short TTL in process cache, or copies under suffixed keys on several shards
fields.Correct: Replicate that key: a short TTL in process cache, or copies under suffixed keys on several shards
fields.Explanation: A single key always maps to one shard, so adding shards or changing the hashing scheme still routes all 500k reads to one node. Spreading copies (key#1 to key#N read randomly) or a local cache in the app tier splits the load. Write through changes write behaviour, not read load on the key.
fields.Hint: One key, one shard, whatever the ring.
fields.Source:
Scaling Memcache at Facebook (https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi13/technical-sessions/presentation/nishtala)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: View counters receive 1 million increments per second. The database handles 20,000 writes per second, and losing a few seconds of counts on a crash is acceptable. Which cache write strategy fits?
fields.Choices:
Write through: update the cache and the database on every increment
Cache aside: write the database, then delete the key
Write back: increment in the cache and flush aggregated counts periodically
Read through: let the cache load counters on miss
fields.Correct: Write back: increment in the cache and flush aggregated counts periodically
fields.Explanation: Write back (write behind) absorbs the 1M/s in memory and turns them into a small number of batched writes, at the cost of losing unflushed data on a crash, which the constraints allow. Write through and cache aside both send every increment to the database, 50x its capacity. Read through only describes the read path.
fields.Hint: The database cannot see every increment.
fields.Source: The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

fields.Question: A chat app stores messages. The main query is "latest 50 messages in conversation X", and group chats have up to 1,000 members. What is the shard key for messages?
fields.Choices:
Message id
Conversation id
Message timestamp
Sender user id
fields.Correct: Conversation id
fields.Explanation: Sharding by conversation id puts every message of a conversation on one shard, so the main query hits one partition, as Discord does with channel plus time bucket. Message id scatters a conversation across all shards. Timestamp makes the newest shard take every write. Sender id splits a group conversation across up to 1,000 shards.
fields.Hint: Shard by what you query by.
fields.Source:
How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages (https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-trillions-of-messages)
Sharding pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding)

fields.Question: A cache cluster places keys with hash(key) mod N on 10 nodes. You add an 11th node. Roughly what fraction of keys move?
fields.Choices:
About 91%
About 9%
About 50%
None, existing keys stay put
fields.Correct: About 91%
fields.Explanation: A key stays only if hash mod 10 equals hash mod 11, which holds for about 10 in 110 values, so about 91% move and the cache effectively goes cold. About 9% (1/11) is what consistent hashing would move. 50% is a guess with no basis. Mod N placement has no notion of keys staying put.
fields.Hint: Compare h mod 10 and h mod 11.
fields.Source:
Consistent Hashing and Random Trees (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/258533.258660)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A consistent hash ring has 4 physical nodes. Load is uneven, and when a node fails its whole range lands on a single neighbour. What fixes both?
fields.Choices:
Raise the replication factor
Switch to range partitioning
Use a larger hash space
Give each node many virtual nodes on the ring
fields.Correct: Give each node many virtual nodes on the ring
fields.Explanation: With many virtual nodes per server, each server owns many small ranges, so load evens out and a failed node's ranges spread over all survivors. Replication adds copies but the neighbour still inherits the range. Range partitioning has its own hot spot problems and does not spread failover. A larger hash space does not change how few points the 4 nodes occupy.
fields.Source:
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
Consistent Hashing and Random Trees (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/258533.258660)

fields.Question: An orders table is range partitioned on created_at. All writes land on the newest partition and it is saturated. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Add read replicas to the newest partition
Move the newest partition to a bigger machine
Partition by a hash of order id or customer id
Range partition on the auto increment order id instead
fields.Correct: Partition by a hash of order id or customer id
fields.Explanation: A monotonic key concentrates every insert on the latest range. Hashing a high cardinality key spreads writes across all partitions. Read replicas do not take writes. A bigger machine buys time but the hot spot remains. An auto increment id is just as monotonic as a timestamp.
fields.Hint: Monotonic keys always hit the end.
fields.Source:
Sharding pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/sharding)
Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Question: A DynamoDB table keyed by user id receives most of its writes on one celebrity's key, throttling that partition. Reads of that user's data can tolerate fanning out. What is the standard fix?
fields.Choices:
Increase table capacity
Write sharding: append a random suffix 0 to N to the key and read all N on query
Add a global secondary index on the user id
Turn on strongly consistent reads
fields.Correct: Write sharding: append a random suffix 0 to N to the key and read all N on query
fields.Explanation: Per partition throughput is capped, so table capacity does not help a single hot key. Suffixing spreads one logical key over N partitions, and the reader merges N results. A GSI with the same key has the same hot spot. Consistency mode does not change write distribution.
fields.Source: Amazon DynamoDB: Using write sharding to distribute workloads evenly (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-sharding.html)

fields.Question: A user edits their profile, reloads and sees the old value because reads go to async replicas. Other users may lag a few seconds. What fixes it with the least cost?
fields.Choices:
Route that user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write
Make every replica synchronous
Read from a random replica and retry until the value changes
Put a cache in front of the replicas
fields.Correct: Route that user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write
fields.Explanation: Read your writes only needs to hold for the writer, so pinning their reads to the leader (or a replica caught up to their write position) for a short window is enough. Synchronous replication fixes it for everyone at a large write latency cost. Retrying until it changes cannot tell an unchanged value from lag. A cache in front adds another stale copy.
fields.Hint: Only one user needs the guarantee.
fields.Source:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)
The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

fields.Question: A leader with asynchronous replication crashes and a follower is promoted. What is the risk?
fields.Choices:
None, followers replay the leader's WAL from disk
The followers cannot be promoted until the old leader returns
Reads after failover become strongly consistent
Writes the old leader acknowledged but had not replicated are lost
fields.Correct: Writes the old leader acknowledged but had not replicated are lost
fields.Explanation: Async replication acknowledges before followers have the write, so failover can drop the tail, and if the old leader comes back it may hold conflicting writes (split brain). Followers only have what was shipped, not the dead leader's local WAL. Promotion does not need the old leader. Failover does not upgrade consistency.
fields.Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Users in the US and EU mostly write from their home region. Write latency must stay low, cross region RTT is 80 ms, and losing a few seconds of writes in a regional disaster is acceptable. Which setup fits?
fields.Choices:
Synchronously commit every write in both regions
One global leader in the US for all writes
Home each user in one region and replicate asynchronously to the other
Active active on all tables with last write wins
fields.Correct: Home each user in one region and replicate asynchronously to the other
fields.Explanation: Homing users keeps writes local, and async replication gives a small RPO, which the constraints accept. Synchronous commits add at least 80 ms to every write. A single US leader makes EU writes slow and a US outage stops all writes. Last write wins across regions silently drops concurrent updates.
fields.Hint: Seconds of RPO is allowed, latency is not.
fields.Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Events for each order must be processed in order, and the topic must handle 100k events per second across many consumers. What do you do?
fields.Choices:
Use a single partition topic
Use the order id as the partition key
Have consumers sort events by timestamp
Add more consumers than partitions
fields.Correct: Use the order id as the partition key
fields.Explanation: Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, and keying by order id sends all events of an order to one partition while different orders spread across many. One partition preserves order but caps throughput at one consumer. Sorting by timestamp in consumers breaks with clock skew and events in flight. Extra consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.
fields.Source: Apache Kafka Documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)

fields.Question: A topic has 12 partitions. A consumer group has 20 consumers. How many consumers receive messages?
fields.Explanation: Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a group, so at most 12 are active and 8 are idle standbys. 20 assumes partitions are shared. 8 is the idle count. 1 confuses consumer groups with a single consumer.
fields.Hint: One partition, one consumer per group.
fields.Source: Apache Kafka Documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)

fields.Question: Producers enqueue faster than consumers can process for hours at a time. The queue keeps growing and end to end latency is now hours. What is the right response?
fields.Choices:
Make the queue unbounded on disk so nothing is ever rejected
Silently drop the oldest messages
Increase producer retries
Bound the queue and push back on producers while scaling consumers
fields.Correct: Bound the queue and push back on producers while scaling consumers
fields.Explanation: A queue smooths bursts but cannot fix sustained overload; backpressure (rejecting or slowing producers with a clear signal) keeps latency bounded while consumers scale. An unbounded queue just converts overload into unbounded latency. Dropping silently loses data no one knows about. More producer retries add load.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload (https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

fields.Question: One malformed message makes the consumer throw every time, so it is redelivered forever and nothing behind it is processed. What is the standard fix?
fields.Choices:
Retry it forever with a longer delay
Skip it without recording anything
After N failed attempts move it to a dead letter queue and keep going
Restart the consumer process
fields.Correct: After N failed attempts move it to a dead letter queue and keep going
fields.Explanation: A dead letter queue isolates poison messages for inspection and replay while the main flow continues. Retrying forever keeps blocking. Skipping loses the message and the evidence. Restarting redelivers the same message.
fields.Hint: Park it, do not lose it.
fields.Source: Amazon SQS dead-letter queues (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html)

fields.Question: An SQS consumer takes 5 minutes per job and deletes the message on success. The visibility timeout is 30 seconds. Jobs are processed twice while the first run is still going. Why?
fields.Choices:
SQS standard queues never redeliver, so the producer sent it twice
The message became visible again after 30 seconds and another consumer received it
The consumer must ack within 1 second
Only FIFO queues delete messages
fields.Correct: The message became visible again after 30 seconds and another consumer received it
fields.Explanation: Visibility timeout hides a received message only for that long; if processing is longer, the message reappears. Set it above the processing time or extend it while working, and keep handlers idempotent since standard queues are at least once anyway. Standard queues do redeliver. There is no 1 second ack rule. Both queue types support delete.
fields.Source: Amazon SQS visibility timeout (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-visibility-timeout.html)

fields.Question: A consumer uses Kafka transactions (exactly once semantics) and sends one email per event. Can a user get the email twice?
fields.Choices:
Yes: exactly once covers Kafka reads and writes, not the email, so dedupe by event id
No, exactly once semantics guarantee the email is sent once
No, as long as the producer uses acks=all
Only if the producer is not idempotent
fields.Correct: Yes: exactly once covers Kafka reads and writes, not the email, so dedupe by event id
fields.Explanation: Kafka EOS makes consume, process and produce atomic within Kafka. If the consumer sends the email and crashes before committing, it reprocesses and sends again. External side effects need their own idempotency, such as recording the event id with the send. acks=all is about durability. Producer idempotence prevents duplicate writes to Kafka, not duplicate emails.
fields.Source: Apache Kafka Documentation (https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/)

fields.Question: An order service must write the order row and publish an OrderCreated event. Neither may happen without the other. What is the standard pattern?
fields.Choices:
Two phase commit between the database and Kafka
Publish to Kafka first, then write the row
Write the row, then publish in the same request handler
Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction, and a relay publishes it
fields.Correct: Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction, and a relay publishes it
fields.Explanation: The outbox makes the event part of the local database transaction; a relay or CDC publishes it at least once, so consumers dedupe. Most brokers do not take part in 2PC with your database, and 2PC adds blocking failures. Publish first leaves an event for an order that may fail to commit. Publish after commit loses the event if the process dies in between.
fields.Source: Pattern: Transactional outbox (https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html)

fields.Question: A client charges a card, times out before seeing the response and retries. The charge must happen once. What do you build?
fields.Choices:
Dedupe on amount and timestamp
Rely on Kafka exactly once delivery
An idempotency key stored with the result, returning the stored result on retry
Two phase commit with the card network
fields.Correct: An idempotency key stored with the result, returning the stored result on retry
fields.Explanation: The client sends a unique key; the server records it atomically with the outcome and replays the saved response on retry, which is how Stripe works. Amount and timestamp collide for real repeat purchases and differ across retries. Kafka EOS does not cover an external charge. Card networks do not take part in your 2PC.
fields.Source:
Stripe API: Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

fields.Question: A request reuses an idempotency key from an earlier request, but the amount is different. What should the API do?
fields.Choices:
Process it as a new charge
Return an error because the parameters do not match the original request
Return the original result without comment
Overwrite the stored result with the new request
fields.Correct: Return an error because the parameters do not match the original request
fields.Explanation: Stripe compares the new parameters with the original and errors on mismatch, since reusing a key for a different operation is a client bug. Processing it defeats the key. Returning the old result hides the bug and the client thinks it charged a new amount. Overwriting breaks the guarantee for the original request.
fields.Hint: Same key, different request means a bug.
fields.Source: Stripe API: Idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)

fields.Question: A Dynamo style store has N = 3 replicas with strict quorums. Which setting guarantees a read sees the latest acknowledged write?
fields.Explanation: Reads overlap writes when R + W is greater than N. 2 + 2 = 4 is greater than 3. 1 + 1, 2 + 1 and 1 + 2 all equal at most 3, so a read can hit only replicas that missed the write. Sloppy quorums and hinted handoff weaken even R + W greater than N.
fields.Hint: Read and write sets must overlap.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: The link between two datacenters is cut. Both sides must keep accepting writes. What do you give up?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, a CA system handles this
Availability, because 2PC keeps both sides consistent
Nothing, Raft keeps both sides writable and consistent
Linearizability: both sides accept writes and reconcile later
fields.Correct: Linearizability: both sides accept writes and reconcile later
fields.Explanation: During a partition you choose consistency or availability; staying writable on both sides means the sides diverge until reconciliation. CA is not a real choice when partitions happen. 2PC blocks during a partition, so it cannot keep both sides writable. Raft only lets the majority side write.
fields.Source:
Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/564585.564601)
Jepsen: Consistency Models (https://jepsen.io/consistency)

fields.Question: Which of these can safely be eventually consistent?
fields.Choices:
Account balance used to approve withdrawals
Seat inventory during checkout
Like count shown on a post
Claims on unique usernames
fields.Correct: Like count shown on a post
fields.Explanation: A like count that lags by a few seconds harms nobody. A balance that lags allows overdrafts. Seat inventory that lags oversells. Usernames need a single authority or two people get the same name.
fields.Hint: What breaks if it is a few seconds stale?
fields.Source: The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

fields.Choices:
Run it inside a transaction at READ COMMITTED
A conditional update that also requires status = 'free' and checks rows affected
Cache the seat status in Redis
Retry the update if it raises an error
fields.Correct: A conditional update that also requires status = 'free' and checks rows affected
fields.Explanation: Both requests read free before either writes. UPDATE seats SET status='held' WHERE id=? AND status='free' makes check and write one atomic step; zero rows affected means someone else won. READ COMMITTED does not stop two transactions reading the same free row. A cache adds another stale copy. Neither update errors, so retry never triggers.
fields.Hint: Make the check part of the write.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Design Ticketmaster (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/ticketmaster)
PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: A wiki page editor: users spend minutes editing, conflicts are rare, and you must not lose an edit silently. What concurrency control fits?
fields.Choices:
Optimistic concurrency: save with WHERE version = the version read, and reject on mismatch
SELECT FOR UPDATE held while the user edits
Last write wins
A Redis lock held for the editing session
fields.Correct: Optimistic concurrency: save with WHERE version = the version read, and reject on mismatch
fields.Explanation: With rare conflicts, a version check at save time costs nothing and turns a conflict into a visible error. Holding a row lock or a distributed lock across minutes of user think time blocks others and leaks when browsers close. Last write wins silently drops the earlier edit.
fields.Source: Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: A worker holds a lock with a 30 second TTL, pauses for 40 seconds in GC, wakes up and writes to storage, overwriting the new lock holder's work. What prevents this?
fields.Choices:
A longer TTL
Redlock across five Redis nodes
A lock with no TTL
Fencing tokens: the lock hands out an increasing number and storage rejects older ones
fields.Correct: Fencing tokens: the lock hands out an increasing number and storage rejects older ones
fields.Explanation: Any pause can outlast a TTL, so the storage must reject the stale writer; a monotonically increasing token checked on each write does that. A longer TTL only needs a longer pause. Redlock still has no fencing, which is Kleppmann's critique. No TTL means a crashed holder blocks forever.
fields.Source: How to do distributed locking (https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html)

fields.Question:
Two requests run this at the same time on a balance of 100, withdrawing 30 and 50. The final balance is 70. What fixes it?
b = SELECT balance FROM acct WHERE id = 1
UPDATE acct SET balance = :b - :amt WHERE id = 1
fields.Choices:
Nothing, READ COMMITTED prevents lost updates
Add an index on acct.id
Do the math in the database: SET balance = balance - :amt
Switch to READ UNCOMMITTED
fields.Correct: Do the math in the database: SET balance = balance - :amt
fields.Explanation: Both read 100 and the second write overwrites the first, a lost update. An atomic UPDATE (or SELECT FOR UPDATE) serializes the change. READ COMMITTED, the PostgreSQL default, does not prevent this pattern. An index speeds lookups but does not lock. READ UNCOMMITTED is weaker, not stronger.
fields.Hint: Read then write in the app is the bug.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL: Transaction Isolation (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html)

fields.Question: A dependency recovers after an outage, and thousands of clients retry and knock it over again. Which retry policy avoids this?
fields.Choices:
Retry immediately
Exponential backoff with random jitter
Retry every 1 second
Exponential backoff without jitter
fields.Correct: Exponential backoff with random jitter
fields.Explanation: Jitter spreads retries in time so clients do not arrive in synchronized waves. Immediate retries hit at full force. A fixed interval keeps every client in lockstep. Backoff without jitter still keeps clients that failed together retrying together.
fields.Source:
Exponential Backoff And Jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/exponential-backoff-and-jitter/)
Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

fields.Question: A request passes through 3 service layers, and each layer makes up to 3 attempts on failure. The bottom database is down. How many calls can one user request make to it?
fields.Explanation: Attempts multiply per layer: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. Retries at every layer turn an outage into a load storm, so retry at one layer and use retry budgets. 9 counts two layers. 3 counts one. 81 adds a fourth layer that does not exist.
fields.Source:
Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)
Site Reliability Engineering: Addressing Cascading Failures (https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

fields.Question: A downstream service starts timing out at 10 seconds. Your request threads pile up waiting and your service stops serving even healthy endpoints. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Raise the timeout to 30 seconds
Add more retries on timeout
Double the thread pool
A circuit breaker that fails fast after an error threshold, plus a shorter timeout
fields.Correct: A circuit breaker that fails fast after an error threshold, plus a shorter timeout
fields.Explanation: A breaker stops calling a failing dependency so threads return immediately and capacity stays available for other work, probing later to close. A longer timeout holds threads longer. Retries add more waiting calls. A bigger pool fills up just the same, only later.
fields.Hint: Stop waiting on something that is down.
fields.Source: CircuitBreaker (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CircuitBreaker.html)

fields.Question: Your service calls a partner API that allows 1,000 requests per second. Your own traffic can spike 100x. What protects the partner and your users?
fields.Choices:
Retry every failure until it succeeds
Autoscale your service to match the spike
Client side rate limit to 1,000 per second with a bounded queue, backoff with jitter and a circuit breaker
Cache every partner response for a day
fields.Correct: Client side rate limit to 1,000 per second with a bounded queue, backoff with jitter and a circuit breaker
fields.Explanation: You must shape your own outbound traffic to the partner's limit and push back when the queue is full. Plain retries multiply load on an already throttled partner. Autoscaling your side sends even more requests. Caching for a day is only valid if responses are cacheable, which the question does not say.
fields.Source:
Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)
Anthropic system design interview (https://www.aced.io/blog/anthropic-system-design-interview)

fields.Question: A server is at 150% of capacity. Latency for every request is climbing past client timeouts. What should it do?
fields.Choices:
Queue everything and process in order
Reject excess requests early, before doing work, and keep serving the rest
Accept everything and let timeouts sort it out
Restart the process to clear the backlog
fields.Correct: Reject excess requests early, before doing work, and keep serving the rest
fields.Explanation: Shedding early (429 or 503, ideally by priority) keeps the accepted requests fast. Queueing everything makes every request late, so clients time out and the work is wasted. Accepting everything is the same failure. Restarting drops in flight work and comes back cold to the same load.
fields.Hint: Serve some well, not all badly.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload (https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

fields.Question: Four instances each run at 80% at peak. One dies, the other three overload and fail one by one. What would have prevented the cascade?
fields.Choices:
Headroom so N minus 1 instances carry peak, plus load shedding above capacity
Autoscaling alone
Faster health checks that eject slow instances
More client retries
fields.Correct: Headroom so N minus 1 instances carry peak, plus load shedding above capacity
fields.Explanation: Losing one of four at 80% puts 107% on each survivor. N minus 1 capacity and shedding keep survivors up. Autoscaling takes minutes to add capacity while the cascade takes seconds. Ejecting slow instances concentrates load on fewer nodes, speeding the cascade. Retries add load.
fields.Hint: Do the math with one instance gone.
fields.Source: Site Reliability Engineering: Addressing Cascading Failures (https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/)

fields.Question: A multi tenant job service has one shared FIFO queue. One customer submits 100,000 jobs and everyone else waits hours. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Keep the shared FIFO and add more workers
Prioritize the smallest jobs first
Reject jobs from all tenants when the queue is long
Per tenant queues or quotas with fair scheduling across tenants
fields.Correct: Per tenant queues or quotas with fair scheduling across tenants
fields.Explanation: Fair share across tenants bounds one tenant's impact regardless of their volume. More workers help until the next bigger burst, which still lands at the head. Shortest first starves large jobs and ignores tenants. Rejecting everyone punishes the tenants who did nothing.
fields.Source:
Fairness in multi-tenant systems (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/fairness-in-multi-tenant-systems/)
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)

fields.Question: A client gives up after 1 second. Service A calls B, which calls C. B and C keep working for 5 more seconds after the client is gone. What fixes this?
fields.Choices:
Give every hop its own 1 second timeout
Remove timeouts and rely on TCP
Propagate the remaining deadline so each hop stops when the budget runs out
Give downstream hops longer timeouts than upstream
fields.Correct: Propagate the remaining deadline so each hop stops when the budget runs out
fields.Explanation: Passing the remaining deadline (as gRPC does) lets each service cancel work nobody will read. Separate 1 second timeouts per hop can add up to 3 seconds and do not shrink. TCP has no request deadline. Longer downstream timeouts guarantee wasted work.
fields.Hint: The budget shrinks at every hop.
fields.Source: gRPC: Deadlines (https://grpc.io/docs/guides/deadlines/)

fields.Question: A dependency's p99 latency is 200 ms, its median 40 ms, and it occasionally hangs forever. You call it with no timeout. What timeout do you set?
fields.Choices:
No timeout, wait for the response
A little above p99, such as 300 to 500 ms
30 seconds to be safe
30 ms, below the median
fields.Correct: A little above p99, such as 300 to 500 ms
fields.Explanation: A timeout just above p99 fails only the truly stuck calls while freeing threads quickly. No timeout lets hung calls hold threads forever. 30 seconds lets a hang tie up threads for half a minute. 30 ms fails most healthy calls.
fields.Hint: Measure, then set it above p99.
fields.Source: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/)

fields.Question: p95 latency on your API doubled an hour ago and p50 is unchanged. Walk through how you find the cause.
fields.Answer:
• Scope: which endpoints, tenants, regions, hosts. Only p95 moving suggests a subset: one shard, one tenant, one dependency, GC, or a slow host.
  • Correlate with changes: deploys, config, traffic mix, a big tenant onboarding.
  • Traces: pick slow requests, find the span that grew (database, cache miss, downstream call, queue wait).
  • Saturation: CPU, GC pauses, connection pool waits, thread pool queueing, disk, hot partition.
  • Mitigate first: roll back, shed or isolate the tenant, drain the bad host; then root cause.

Strong answers separate mitigation from root cause and explain why a tail only shift points to a subset.
fields.Source:
Anthropic system design interview (https://www.aced.io/blog/anthropic-system-design-interview)
Site Reliability Engineering: Handling Overload (https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)

fields.Question: Your design runs in one region and the interviewer says "that region just went down". How does the design change?
fields.Answer:
• Decide RTO and RPO with the interviewer: minutes of downtime, seconds of data loss?
  • Stateless tier: deploy in a second region behind global DNS or anycast load balancing.
  • Data: async replicas in the second region (small RPO) or synchronous or consensus based replication across regions (zero RPO, higher write latency).
  • Failover: automated health checks, promotion, fencing the old leader to avoid split brain, and a tested runbook.
  • Capacity: the survivor must carry full load.

Name the tradeoff: active passive is simpler, active active needs conflict handling or per user homing.
fields.Hint: Ask for RTO and RPO first.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Amazon L6 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/amazon/l6)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: Billions of chat messages, append heavy, always queried as "messages in conversation X by time", no joins. Which store fits best?
fields.Choices:
A single PostgreSQL instance
A graph database
Wide column store partitioned by conversation and time bucket
Elasticsearch as the primary store
fields.Correct: Wide column store partitioned by conversation and time bucket
fields.Explanation: Wide column stores (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable) handle huge append rates and serve one partition sorted by time, which is exactly the access pattern, as Discord does. One PostgreSQL instance will not hold billions of rows at this write rate. A graph database optimizes traversals you do not need. Elasticsearch is a search index, not a durable primary for this.
fields.Hint: Match the store to the access pattern.
fields.Source:
How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages (https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-trillions-of-messages)
Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Question: The hot query is: WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Which index serves it best?
fields.Choices:
An index on created_at only
A composite index on (user_id, created_at)
Separate indexes on user_id and on created_at
A composite index on (created_at, user_id)
fields.Correct: A composite index on (user_id, created_at)
fields.Explanation: Equality column first, then the sort column, lets the database seek to the user and read 20 rows already in order. created_at alone scans recent rows for all users. Two separate indexes need a merge and a sort. (created_at, user_id) puts the range column first, so it cannot seek by user.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL: Multicolumn Indexes (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-multicolumn.html)

fields.Question: A browser dashboard shows live prices. Data flows only server to client, it must work over ordinary HTTP, and you want built in reconnection. Which transport fits?
fields.Choices:
Server-sent events
Short polling every 100 ms
WebSockets
Long polling
fields.Correct: Server-sent events
fields.Explanation: SSE is a one way stream over plain HTTP with automatic reconnect and Last-Event-ID built into EventSource. Short polling at 100 ms wastes requests. WebSockets work but are bidirectional and need your own reconnect logic. Long polling reconnects after every message, adding latency and overhead.
fields.Hint: One way, plain HTTP, reconnect included.
fields.Source: MDN: Using server-sent events (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events)

fields.Question: You need to send /api traffic to one service pool and /static to another, based on the URL path. Which load balancer?
fields.Choices:
Layer 4 (TCP) load balancer
DNS round robin
Anycast IP
Layer 7 (HTTP) load balancer
fields.Correct: Layer 7 (HTTP) load balancer
fields.Explanation: Only an L7 balancer parses HTTP and can route on path. L4 sees ports and IPs, not URLs. DNS round robin picks a host before any request is sent. Anycast routes to the nearest site by network, not by path.
fields.Source: The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)

fields.Question: Product images are served worldwide from one origin, and users far away see slow loads. Images rarely change. What is the fix?
fields.Choices:
Move the origin to a bigger machine
Add database read replicas
Serve them through a CDN with long cache lifetimes and versioned URLs
Cache images in app server memory
fields.Correct: Serve them through a CDN with long cache lifetimes and versioned URLs
fields.Explanation: A CDN puts copies near users, and versioned file names let you cache for a year and still ship changes instantly. A bigger origin does not shorten the distance. Database replicas have nothing to do with image bytes. App server memory is still in one region.
fields.Source:
The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
MDN: HTTP caching (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching)

fields.Question: Chat users hold WebSockets to 50 gateway servers. User A on gateway 3 messages user B on gateway 41. How does the message reach B?
fields.Choices:
Sticky sessions on the load balancer
A connection registry or pub/sub channel keyed by user routes it to B's gateway
Broadcast every message to all 50 gateways
Have B poll the database every second
fields.Correct: A connection registry or pub/sub channel keyed by user routes it to B's gateway
fields.Explanation: You need to know or subscribe to where B is connected: a registry (user to gateway) or a per user pub/sub topic. Sticky sessions keep A on one gateway but do nothing to find B. Broadcasting to all gateways multiplies traffic by 50. Polling defeats the point of WebSockets.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Hello Interview: System Design in a Hurry (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/introduction)

fields.Question: Ad clicks must be counted per minute by when the click happened. Up to 2% of events arrive as late as 2 minutes. What windowing works?
fields.Choices:
Event time tumbling windows with a watermark allowing about 2 minutes of lateness
Processing time windows
Event time windows that drop anything late
A nightly batch job only
fields.Correct: Event time tumbling windows with a watermark allowing about 2 minutes of lateness
fields.Explanation: Event time assigns clicks to the minute they happened, and the watermark keeps windows open long enough for late data. Processing time counts arrival minute, misplacing late clicks. Dropping late events loses 2% of billable clicks. A nightly batch is accurate but fails the per minute need.
fields.Source:
Apache Flink: Timely Stream Processing (https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-stable/docs/concepts/time/)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A users table is sharded by user_id. Login needs lookup by email at 100k QPS. What do you add?
fields.Choices:
Query every shard for each login
Also shard the users table by email
Cache the full users table in every app server
A separate index (email to user_id) partitioned by email
fields.Correct: A separate index (email to user_id) partitioned by email
fields.Explanation: A global index partitioned by the lookup key turns the email lookup into one read plus one read by user_id. Scatter gather to every shard at 100k QPS multiplies load by the shard count. A table can only be partitioned one way. Caching the whole table everywhere does not scale and goes stale.
fields.Source:
Amazon DynamoDB: Using Global Secondary Indexes (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/GSI.html)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (https://dataintensive.net/)

fields.Question: A rate limiter for a 50k QPS API on 40 nodes: limits must be global per user, short bursts allowed. Which design?
fields.Choices:
In memory counters on each node
Fixed window counter per minute
Token bucket per user in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script
A SQL row insert per request, counted per user
fields.Correct: Token bucket per user in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script
fields.Explanation: A shared token bucket enforces one global limit and allows bursts up to bucket size; Lua keeps refill and take atomic. Per node counters let a user get 40x the limit by spreading requests. Fixed windows allow up to 2x the limit at a window edge. A SQL insert per request at 50k QPS is too slow and grows forever.
fields.Source:
Scaling your API with rate limiters (https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A fixed window limiter allows 100 requests per minute, windows starting on the minute. What is the most a client can send in 2 seconds?
fields.Explanation: Send 100 at 0:59 and 100 at 1:00; each window sees exactly 100. Sliding window or token bucket fixes this. 100 assumes windows slide. 101 and 150 have no basis in the window math.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question:
Clients exceed the limit under concurrency. What is wrong?
count = int(redis.get(key) or 0)
if count < LIMIT:
    redis.set(key, count + 1, ex=60)
    allow()
fields.Choices:
GET and SET are separate, so concurrent requests read the same count; use INCR or a Lua script
Nothing, Redis is single threaded so this is safe
The TTL should be longer than 60 seconds
It needs a local in memory cache in front
fields.Correct: GET and SET are separate, so concurrent requests read the same count; use INCR or a Lua script
fields.Explanation: Single threaded means each command is atomic, not a sequence of commands. Two requests can both GET 5 and both SET 6. INCR returns the new value atomically, with EXPIRE on the first increment, or do it in Lua. This code also resets the TTL on every SET. A longer TTL does not fix the race. A local cache makes counts less accurate.
fields.Hint: Atomic per command, not per function.
fields.Source: Redis: INCR, pattern: rate limiter (https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/incr/)

fields.Question: Design a distributed rate limiter for a public API. Give requirements, the algorithm and two deep dives.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: per user or key limits, global across nodes, low added latency (under a few ms), fail open or closed decided up front, clear 429 with Retry-After.
  • Algorithm: token bucket (bursts) or sliding window counter (smooth), state in Redis keyed by client, updated in a Lua script.
  • Placement: API gateway or middleware before business logic.
  • Deep dive 1, scale: shard Redis by key, local pre-check or batching for hot keys, accept slight overrun.
  • Deep dive 2, failure: Redis down means fail open for most APIs (availability) or closed for abuse sensitive ones, with local fallback limits.

Mention multi region: per region limits or async sync of counters with tolerance.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Scaling your API with rate limiters (https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)

fields.Question: A URL shortener creates billions of codes on many writer nodes. Codes must never collide and should be short. How do you generate them?
fields.Choices:
Hash the long URL and keep the first 7 characters
One auto increment column in a single database
Hand each node unique counter ranges (or Snowflake style IDs) and base62 encode
Random UUIDv4 for each code
fields.Correct: Hand each node unique counter ranges (or Snowflake style IDs) and base62 encode
fields.Explanation: Disjoint ranges or Snowflake IDs are unique without coordination per request, and base62 keeps them short. Truncated hashes collide and need a check and retry. A single auto increment database is a bottleneck and single point of failure. A UUID is 36 characters, defeating the short URL.
fields.Hint: Unique without asking anyone each time.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Announcing Snowflake (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/a/2010/announcing-snowflake)

fields.Question: Your shortener must record every click for analytics. Which redirect status do you return?
fields.Choices:
301 Moved Permanently
302 Found
308 Permanent Redirect
200 with an HTML meta refresh
fields.Correct: 302 Found
fields.Explanation: 302 is temporary, so browsers come back to you on every click. 301 and 308 are permanent and cacheable by default, so repeat clicks skip your server and are not counted. A 200 with meta refresh is slower, worse for clients and crawlers, and not a redirect.
fields.Source:
RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: You need room for 100 billion short codes using base62 characters. What is the minimum code length?
fields.Explanation: 62^6 is about 57 billion, too few. 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion, enough. 8 and 10 work but are longer than needed.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly. Requirements, API, data model and the two deep dives.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: create short URL, redirect, optional custom alias and expiry. Read heavy (100:1), redirect p99 low.
  • API: POST /urls {longUrl} returns code; GET /{code} returns 302.
  • Data: code to long URL, owner, created, expiry. Key value store or sharded SQL keyed by code.
  • Deep dive 1, IDs: counter ranges or Snowflake, base62, 7 characters.
  • Deep dive 2, reads: cache code lookups (cache aside, LRU), CDN or edge caching, async click logging through a queue.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
Hello Interview: Amazon L6 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/amazon/l6)

fields.Question: Each cache node needs O(1) get, O(1) put and LRU eviction. Which structure?
fields.Choices:
Min heap keyed by last access time
Array sorted by last access time
Hash map plus doubly linked list
Hash map alone, scanning for the oldest on eviction
fields.Correct: Hash map plus doubly linked list
fields.Explanation: The map finds the node, the list moves it to the front and pops the tail, all O(1), which is what OrderedDict gives you. A heap needs O(log n) per access update. A sorted array needs O(n) moves. Scanning on eviction is O(n).
fields.Source: Python documentation: collections.OrderedDict (https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.OrderedDict)

fields.Question: A single node LSM key value store writes to its WAL with fsync, updates the memtable and acks. It crashes before flushing the memtable. Why is no acked data lost?
fields.Choices:
The memtable is stored on disk
The WAL is replayed on restart to rebuild the memtable
Replicas hold the data
SSTables are written on every put
fields.Correct: The WAL is replayed on restart to rebuild the memtable
fields.Explanation: The write ahead log is the durable copy until the memtable flushes to an SSTable. The memtable is in memory. The question says single node, so there are no replicas. SSTables are written on flush, not per put, which is what makes LSM writes fast.
fields.Hint: What hit the disk before the ack?
fields.Source:
The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) (https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf)
Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Question: An LSM store keeps a Bloom filter per SSTable. What does it do on a read?
fields.Choices:
Skips SSTables that definitely do not contain the key
Tells exactly which SSTable has the key
Compresses the SSTable keys
Keeps keys sorted inside the SSTable
fields.Correct: Skips SSTables that definitely do not contain the key
fields.Explanation: A Bloom filter has no false negatives and some false positives, so it can rule out SSTables and save disk reads, but a yes is only a maybe. It cannot point to the one table that has the key. Compression and sort order are separate parts of the SSTable format.
fields.Source:
Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362686.362692)
Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (https://research.google/pubs/bigtable-a-distributed-storage-system-for-structured-data/)

fields.Question: A shopping cart store must accept writes during a network partition, and an item added on either side must never be lost. How do you resolve concurrent versions?
fields.Choices:
Last write wins by timestamp
Reject writes on the minority side
Route all writes to a single leader
Track versions with vector clocks and merge the siblings (union of items)
fields.Correct: Track versions with vector clocks and merge the siblings (union of items)
fields.Explanation: Vector clocks detect concurrent versions and the application merges them, which is Dynamo's cart design. Last write wins discards one side's item. Rejecting writes or requiring a leader breaks the always writable requirement.
fields.Source: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)

fields.Question: Design a distributed key value store. Requirements, partitioning, replication and the write and read paths.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: get and put, large data, tunable consistency, high availability.
  • Partitioning: consistent hashing with virtual nodes.
  • Replication: N replicas on the next distinct nodes; quorum R and W with R + W greater than N for strong reads.
  • Write path: WAL, memtable, flush to SSTables, compaction.
  • Read path: memtable, then SSTables with Bloom filters.
  • Failures: hinted handoff, read repair, anti entropy with Merkle trees, gossip membership.
  • Conflicts: vector clocks or last write wins, chosen per use case.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf)
The Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) (https://www.cs.umb.edu/~poneil/lsmtree.pdf)

fields.Question: Why do Twitter style Snowflake IDs fit tweet IDs better than UUIDv4?
fields.Choices:
They are strictly sequential across all machines
They are 64 bit and roughly time sortable, generated without coordination
They do not depend on the clock
They are shorter because they use base64
fields.Correct: They are 64 bit and roughly time sortable, generated without coordination
fields.Explanation: Snowflake packs a timestamp, a worker id and a sequence into 64 bits, so IDs sort by time and fit in a long index column. They are only roughly ordered across machines, not strictly sequential. They depend heavily on the clock. Encoding is not what makes them short, the 64 bit size is.
fields.Source: Announcing Snowflake (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/a/2010/announcing-snowflake)

fields.Question: An NTP adjustment moves a Snowflake worker's clock back 50 ms. What should the generator do?
fields.Choices:
Refuse to generate (or wait) until the clock passes the last timestamp used
Keep generating with the current time
Reset the sequence number to 0 and continue
Use the last timestamp minus 1
fields.Correct: Refuse to generate (or wait) until the clock passes the last timestamp used
fields.Explanation: Generating with an earlier timestamp can reproduce IDs already issued in that millisecond, so the generator must wait or error. Keeping on or resetting the sequence risks exact duplicates. Going further back makes it worse.
fields.Source: Announcing Snowflake (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/a/2010/announcing-snowflake)

fields.Question: Messages in a conversation must appear in the same order on every device. What provides that order?
fields.Choices:
Client device timestamps
Server arrival timestamps across all servers
One global sequence for all messages
A per conversation sequence number assigned where the conversation is owned
fields.Correct: A per conversation sequence number assigned where the conversation is owned
fields.Explanation: One owner per conversation (its partition or leader) can assign a monotonically increasing sequence, and clients sort by it. Client clocks skew and can be set to anything. Wall clocks on different servers also drift. A global sequence is a needless bottleneck when ordering only matters within a conversation.
fields.Hint: Order only matters within a conversation.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages (https://discord.com/blog/how-discord-stores-trillions-of-messages)

fields.Question: A phone was offline for 2 hours. On reconnect, how does it get exactly the messages it missed?
fields.Choices:
The server resends every message in every conversation
Push notifications carry the missed messages
It sends its last seen sequence per conversation and the server returns everything after
The client asks for messages newer than its own clock
fields.Correct: It sends its last seen sequence per conversation and the server returns everything after
fields.Explanation: A sync cursor makes catch up cheap and exact. Resending everything wastes bandwidth. Push delivery is best effort and coalesced, not a reliable transport. Client clocks are skewed, so a time based query misses or repeats messages.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: You show online status. Clients can vanish without disconnecting (dead battery, tunnel). How do you detect offline?
fields.Choices:
Mark offline only on explicit logout
Clients heartbeat every few seconds and are marked offline when the heartbeat TTL expires
Poll the database for each user's last login
Rely on default TCP keepalive
fields.Correct: Clients heartbeat every few seconds and are marked offline when the heartbeat TTL expires
fields.Explanation: Heartbeats with a TTL (for example in Redis) catch silent disappearances within seconds. Users rarely log out. Last login says nothing about now. Default TCP keepalive waits around 2 hours before probing.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Design WhatsApp or Slack messaging. Requirements, connection model, storage and two deep dives.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: 1:1 and group chat, delivery and read receipts, offline delivery, multi device, ordering per conversation.
  • Connections: WebSocket gateways, registry of user to gateway, pub/sub between gateways.
  • Storage: messages in a wide column store partitioned by conversation id, sorted by sequence.
  • Deep dive 1, delivery: client message id for dedupe on retry, ack flow, per device sync cursor, push via APNs or FCM when offline.
  • Deep dive 2, large groups: write once per conversation, fan out notifications to online members only, rate limits for huge channels.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Hello Interview: Amazon L6 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/amazon/l6)
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)

fields.Question: A feed service: average user has 200 followers, a few accounts have 50 million, reads far outnumber writes. Which fanout?
fields.Choices:
Push every post to every follower's timeline
Pull and merge from all followees on every read
Store one global timeline and filter per user
Hybrid: push to followers' timelines for normal users, pull celebrity posts at read time
fields.Correct: Hybrid: push to followers' timelines for normal users, pull celebrity posts at read time
fields.Explanation: Push makes reads cheap for the common case; pulling the few celebrity accounts at read avoids 50 million writes per post, which is Twitter's approach. Pure push melts on celebrity posts. Pure pull makes every read merge hundreds of sources. A global timeline filtered per user does not scale.
fields.Hint: Treat the 50 million follower accounts differently.
fields.Source:
The Infrastructure Behind Twitter: Scale (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/topics/infrastructure/2017/the-infrastructure-behind-twitter-scale)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Precomputed timelines live in Redis. Why store only post IDs (capped at a few hundred per user) instead of full post bodies?
fields.Choices:
Redis lists cannot hold strings longer than 64 bytes
Full bodies would make timeline reads strongly consistent
IDs keep memory small and edits or deletes apply once in the post store
IDs let you skip the post cache entirely
fields.Correct: IDs keep memory small and edits or deletes apply once in the post store
fields.Explanation: Copying bodies into millions of timelines multiplies memory and makes every edit or delete a fanout. IDs are hydrated from a post cache. Redis strings can be up to 512 MB. Consistency does not come from storing bodies. You still need a post cache to hydrate the IDs.
fields.Hint: Copy the pointer, not the data.
fields.Source: The Infrastructure Behind Twitter: Scale (https://blog.x.com/engineering/en_us/topics/infrastructure/2017/the-infrastructure-behind-twitter-scale)

fields.Question: Design a news feed (Facebook or Twitter home timeline). Requirements, API, fanout choice and deep dives.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: post, follow, read home feed in reverse time or ranked, low read latency, eventual consistency OK.
  • API: POST /posts, GET /feed?cursor=.
  • Fanout: hybrid push for normal users, pull for celebrities; timeline cache of post IDs.
  • Deep dives: celebrity handling, cursor pagination, ranking stage, cache warmup for inactive users, social graph store (TAO style).
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph (https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc13/technical-sessions/presentation/bronson)
Hello Interview: Meta E5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/meta/e5)

fields.Question: Your iOS app is closed. How does your backend notify the user about a new message?
fields.Choices:
Send a push through APNs using the device token
Keep a WebSocket open in the background
Send an SMS for every message
Have the app poll every minute
fields.Correct: Send a push through APNs using the device token
fields.Explanation: Only Apple's push service can wake or alert a closed app; your server sends to APNs with the device token (FCM on Android). iOS suspends background sockets. SMS costs money and is a different channel. A closed app cannot poll.
fields.Source:
Apple Developer: Sending notification requests to APNs (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/sending-notification-requests-to-apns)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A webhook platform: one merchant's endpoint returns 500 for every request, and retries are delaying delivery to all other merchants. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
One global retry queue with a shorter delay
Retry immediately in a loop until it succeeds
Drop the event after the first failure
Per destination queues or rate limits with backoff, and a dead letter queue after N attempts
fields.Correct: Per destination queues or rate limits with backoff, and a dead letter queue after N attempts
fields.Explanation: Isolating by destination stops one bad endpoint from blocking the rest, and backoff plus DLQ bound the work spent on it. A shared retry queue keeps the head of line blocking. Tight retry loops burn workers. Dropping after one failure breaks at least once delivery for transient errors.
fields.Source:
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)
Fairness in multi-tenant systems (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/fairness-in-multi-tenant-systems/)

fields.Question: Customers register webhook URLs that your servers call. An attacker registers a hostname that resolves to 169.254.169.254. What protects you?
fields.Choices:
Require the URL to start with https
Check the hostname once at registration
Resolve and check the IP at send time against private and metadata ranges, through an isolated egress proxy
Allow any URL, since your servers only send POSTs
fields.Correct: Resolve and check the IP at send time against private and metadata ranges, through an isolated egress proxy
fields.Explanation: SSRF is blocked by validating the resolved address on every request (DNS can change after registration) and sending from a network that cannot reach internal services. https does not limit the destination. A registration time check is defeated by DNS rebinding. POST requests to internal endpoints can still do damage.
fields.Hint: Check where it really goes, every time.
fields.Source: OWASP: Server-Side Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Server_Side_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html)

fields.Question: Design a webhook delivery platform (Stripe or OpenAI style). Requirements, delivery semantics and failure handling.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: at least once delivery, per endpoint ordering optional, signed payloads, retries for days, visibility for customers.
  • Flow: events written via outbox, queue, delivery workers, per destination scheduling.
  • Retries: exponential backoff with jitter, DLQ, auto disable broken endpoints with notification, manual replay.
  • Isolation: per merchant concurrency and rate limits so one slow endpoint cannot starve others.
  • Security: HMAC signature with timestamp, SSRF protection on egress.
  • Receivers: must dedupe by event id since delivery is at least once.
fields.Source:
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Ticketing: a user selects a seat and has 10 minutes to pay. If they abandon checkout the seat must become available again. How do you model it?
fields.Choices:
A hold with an expires_at, treated as free once expired, confirmed on payment
Release only when the user clicks cancel
A cron job that releases abandoned holds once a day
Keep the hold in the app server's memory
fields.Correct: A hold with an expires_at, treated as free once expired, confirmed on payment
fields.Explanation: A hold row with an expiry (or a Redis key with TTL) frees the seat automatically and the confirm step checks the hold is still valid. Users who close the tab never click cancel. A daily job leaves seats locked for hours. App memory is lost on restart and invisible to other servers.
fields.Hint: Make the hold expire on its own.
fields.Source: Hello Interview: Design Ticketmaster (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/ticketmaster)

fields.Question: A concert on sale draws 1 million users for 50,000 seats in the first minute. What keeps the booking system up and fair?
fields.Choices:
Autoscale the database
Cache the seat map and let everyone book at once
Let all users race on a database row lock
A virtual waiting room that admits users at a controlled rate
fields.Correct: A virtual waiting room that admits users at a controlled rate
fields.Explanation: A waiting room turns a spike into a steady flow the booking path can handle and gives a fair order. Database autoscaling is slow and contention on the same rows does not scale out. Caching the seat map helps browsing but not 1 million concurrent bookings. Racing on row locks melts the database and is random, not fair.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Design Ticketmaster (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/ticketmaster)
Cloudflare Waiting Room (https://blog.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-waiting-room/)

fields.Question: Design Ticketmaster. Requirements, core entities, API and the deep dives.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: browse and search events, view seat map, book without double booking, handle on sale spikes. Consistency for booking, availability for browsing.
  • Entities: event, venue, seat, ticket, booking.
  • API: GET /events/:id, POST /bookings/hold, POST /bookings/:id/confirm.
  • Deep dive 1, holds: conditional update or Redis lock with TTL, confirm on payment, expire otherwise.
  • Deep dive 2, spikes: virtual waiting room, cached seat map with live updates via SSE.
  • Search: Elasticsearch fed by CDC.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Design Ticketmaster (https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/problem-breakdowns/ticketmaster)
Hello Interview: Meta E5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/meta/e5)
Hello Interview: Google L5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/google/l5)

fields.Question: A wallet system keeps a double entry ledger. Which rule must always hold?
fields.Choices:
Each account's balance column is updated in place on every transaction
Every transaction's entries sum to zero and entries are never edited, only reversed by new entries
Mistaken entries are deleted to keep the ledger clean
Only credits are recorded, debits are derived
fields.Correct: Every transaction's entries sum to zero and entries are never edited, only reversed by new entries
fields.Explanation: Double entry means each movement debits one account and credits another for the same amount, and the log is append only so history is auditable; corrections are new entries. Updating a balance in place without entries loses the audit trail. Deleting entries destroys history. Recording one side only is single entry bookkeeping.
fields.Hint: Money moves, it is never created.
fields.Source:
Accounting for Developers, Part I (https://www.moderntreasury.com/journal/accounting-for-developers-part-i)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Your call to the payment provider timed out, so your database marked the charge failed. The provider actually succeeded. How do you catch and fix this?
fields.Choices:
Reconcile with the provider by idempotency key or settlement report and correct your state
Retry the charge with a new idempotency key
Leave it failed, the provider will refund automatically
Use two phase commit with the provider
fields.Correct: Reconcile with the provider by idempotency key or settlement report and correct your state
fields.Explanation: A timeout is unknown, not failed. Query the provider (same idempotency key) and run periodic reconciliation against settlement files. A new key creates a second real charge. Providers do not refund on your behalf. External providers do not join your 2PC.
fields.Hint: A timeout is not a failure.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)

fields.Question: How should a payments service store the amount 19.99 USD?
fields.Choices:
As a double precision float 19.99
As the string "$19.99"
As a float rounded to 2 decimals on every write
As the integer 1999 in minor units, with the currency code
fields.Correct: As the integer 1999 in minor units, with the currency code
fields.Explanation: Integers in the smallest currency unit add exactly, which is how Stripe's API takes amounts; note some currencies have zero or three decimals. Binary floats cannot represent 0.1 or 19.99 exactly, so sums drift, and rounding each write does not fix accumulation. Strings with symbols need parsing and lose the currency for symbols like $ shared by many currencies.
fields.Source: Stripe: Supported currencies, zero-decimal and minor units (https://docs.stripe.com/currencies)

fields.Question: Checkout calls payment, then inventory, in separate services with their own databases. Payment succeeds, inventory is out of stock. What happens in a saga?
fields.Choices:
Two phase commit rolls back the payment
Ignore it and ship later
A compensating action refunds the payment
Retry inventory until stock appears
fields.Correct: A compensating action refunds the payment
fields.Explanation: Sagas replace a distributed transaction with local steps and explicit compensations. 2PC across microservices is avoided because it blocks and couples availability. Ignoring it takes money for nothing. Retrying forever leaves the customer charged with no order.
fields.Source: Saga distributed transactions pattern (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/saga)

fields.Question: Design a payment system (Stripe like or a checkout backend). Requirements, flow and correctness guarantees.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: charge once, never lose money, auditability, handle provider timeouts.
  • Flow: create payment intent with idempotency key, call provider, record result, emit event via outbox.
  • Ledger: double entry, append only, balances derived.
