  • Correctness: idempotency keys end to end, state machine with unknown state on timeout, reconciliation jobs against provider reports.
  • Failures: retries with the same key, webhooks from the provider deduped, sagas with refunds.

Say explicitly that exactly once delivery does not exist; you get at least once plus idempotency.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency (https://stripe.com/blog/idempotency)
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)

fields.Question: Drivers update location every 4 seconds; riders query drivers within 2 km. Which index fits?
fields.Choices:
Geohash or H3 cells in an in memory store, querying the rider's cell and its neighbours
Latitude and longitude B tree range query in SQL
A quadtree stored in the database and rebuilt per update
Full scan of all drivers per request
fields.Correct: Geohash or H3 cells in an in memory store, querying the rider's cell and its neighbours
fields.Explanation: Cell IDs turn a 2D search into a few key lookups and updates are cheap key moves, which suits high churn. A B tree on lat and long can only range on one dimension efficiently. Rebuilding a quadtree in a database per update is expensive. Full scans do not scale.
fields.Source:
H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index (https://www.uber.com/blog/h3/)
Redis: Geospatial indexes (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A geohash search queries only the rider's own cell and misses a driver 50 meters away. Why, and what fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Geohash precision is too high; use a shorter geohash only
Geohashes are random; switch to UUIDs
The driver's location is stale; poll faster
The driver is in an adjacent cell; also query the 8 neighbouring cells
fields.Correct: The driver is in an adjacent cell; also query the 8 neighbouring cells
fields.Explanation: Points near a boundary can sit in different cells, sometimes with very different prefixes, so you search neighbours too. A shorter geohash alone still has edges. Geohashes are not random. Staleness is a different issue from a 50 meter boundary miss.
fields.Source:
Redis: Geospatial indexes (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/geospatial/)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: 1 million active drivers each send a location every 4 seconds. What write rate must the location service handle?
fields.Choices:
4,000,000 per second
25,000 per second
250,000 per second
1,000,000 per second
fields.Correct: 250,000 per second
fields.Explanation: 1,000,000 / 4 = 250,000 updates per second, which is why locations go to an in memory store rather than a durable row per update. 4,000,000 multiplies by 4. 25,000 drops a zero. 1,000,000 assumes one update per second.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Design Uber's ride matching. Requirements, location ingestion, matching and the deep dives.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: riders request, nearby drivers found in seconds, each driver gets one ride at a time, ETA.
  • Ingestion: drivers push location every few seconds to an in memory geo index (H3 or geohash cells), sharded by region.
  • Matching: query nearby cells, rank by ETA, offer to one driver at a time with a timeout; claim the driver atomically (conditional update or lock with TTL) so no double dispatch.
  • Deep dives: hot cells downtown, surge, driver offline detection, consistency of the trip state machine, payments via the payment system.
fields.Hint: Geo index and atomic driver claim.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index (https://www.uber.com/blog/h3/)
PracHub: Uber system design questions (https://prachub.com/companies/uber/categories/system-design)

fields.Question: Top 100 videos by views over the last hour, billions of events, approximate counts acceptable, memory must be bounded. Which approach?
fields.Choices:
Count-min sketch for counts plus a min heap of size 100
Exact hash map of every video id on one machine
Sort all events each hour
HyperLogLog per video
fields.Correct: Count-min sketch for counts plus a min heap of size 100
fields.Explanation: A count-min sketch gives bounded memory frequency estimates and the heap tracks the current top K. An exact map of every id may not fit and is not bounded. Sorting billions of events hourly is slow and late. HyperLogLog counts distinct items, not how often each occurs.
fields.Source:
An Improved Data Stream Summary: The Count-Min Sketch and its Applications (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jalgor.2003.12.001)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A game has 10 million players and needs live score updates and each player's rank on demand. What fits?
fields.Choices:
SQL ORDER BY score with COUNT on every rank request
A binary heap in the app server
A hash map from player to score
A Redis sorted set with ZINCRBY and ZREVRANK
fields.Correct: A Redis sorted set with ZINCRBY and ZREVRANK
fields.Explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score with O(log n) updates and rank lookups. COUNT of higher scores on every request scans a large range. A heap gives the top but not an arbitrary player's rank. A hash map has no order.
fields.Source:
Redis: Sorted sets (https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/data-types/sorted-sets/)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Events are partitioned randomly across 10 workers. Each sends its local top 10 and you merge them. Is the result the exact global top 10?
fields.Choices:
Yes, the global top 10 is always within the local top 10 lists
Yes, if every worker uses exact counts
No: an item just below the cut on every worker can be globally top; partition by item id instead
No, but adding more workers fixes it
fields.Correct: No: an item just below the cut on every worker can be globally top; partition by item id instead
fields.Explanation: With random partitioning an item's count is split across workers and can miss every local list while its total is high. Partitioning by item id puts each item's full count on one worker, so merging local top K is exact. Exact local counts do not help a split item. More workers split counts further.
fields.Hint: Where does one item's count live?
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Hello Interview: Meta E5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/meta/e5)

fields.Question: Design YouTube top K videos for the last hour, day and month.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: K up to 1,000, windows of 1 hour, 1 day, 1 month, results within a minute, approximate OK for short windows?
  • Ingest: view events to Kafka partitioned by video id.
  • Fast path: stream workers keep per window counts (or count-min plus heap) and publish local top K; merge is exact because partitions are by video.
  • Accurate path: batch job over raw events for exact daily and monthly results.
  • Serve: precomputed lists in a cache.
  • Deep dives: sliding vs tumbling windows, late events, hot videos, cost of month windows (roll up hourly counts).
fields.Hint: Partition by video, fast and accurate paths.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Meta E5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/meta/e5)
Hello Interview: Google L5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/google/l5)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Ad clicks drive billing and must be exact. Dashboards need counts within a minute. What architecture fits?
fields.Choices:
A streaming pipeline for near real time counts plus batch reconciliation from the raw log for billing
Streaming counts only, bill from them directly
Nightly batch only
Count clicks in the ad server's memory and flush hourly
fields.Correct: A streaming pipeline for near real time counts plus batch reconciliation from the raw log for billing
fields.Explanation: Streaming gives fast numbers, while reconciliation over the immutable raw log (with click id dedupe) corrects late, duplicate or replayed events before billing. Streaming alone can drift with late and duplicate events. Batch only misses the minute requirement. In memory counts are lost on crash.
fields.Hint: Fast and exact are two paths.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A metrics system ingests millions of points per second, and users chart 1 year of data at 1 hour resolution. How do you store it?
fields.Choices:
Keep every raw point forever and aggregate at query time
A PostgreSQL row per point with an index on time
Randomly sample 1% of points
Keep raw points for a short retention and roll up to coarser resolutions for long ranges
fields.Correct: Keep raw points for a short retention and roll up to coarser resolutions for long ranges
fields.Explanation: Downsampled rollups keep year long queries cheap while raw data serves recent detailed views; time series databases also compress heavily (Gorilla). Aggregating raw data at query time over a year is slow and storage grows forever. A row per point at millions per second overwhelms a general purpose database. Random sampling loses spikes, the thing you monitor for.
fields.Source:
Gorilla: A Fast, Scalable, In-Memory Time Series Database (https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p1816-teller.pdf)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: An engineer adds a user_id label to a request latency metric with 50 million users. What happens?
fields.Choices:
Nothing, labels are free
Queries get faster because data is more specific
Each user creates a new time series, blowing up memory and index size; use logs or traces for per user data
Only disk use grows, memory is unchanged
fields.Correct: Each user creates a new time series, blowing up memory and index size; use logs or traces for per user data
fields.Explanation: Every unique label combination is a separate series, so 50 million users means at least 50 million series per metric. Prometheus guidance says not to use unbounded labels like user ids. Labels are not free. More series makes queries slower. In memory indexes grow with series count.
fields.Hint: Each label value is a new series.
fields.Source: Prometheus: Metric and label naming (https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/naming/)

fields.Question: Design a metrics monitoring and alerting system (Datadog style).
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: ingest millions of points per second, query recent data in seconds, alert within a minute, retain a year.
  • Ingest: agents push to collectors, Kafka partitioned by series, writes to a time series store.
  • Storage: compressed time series blocks, rollups for older data, cardinality limits per tenant.
  • Query: aggregation by tags, caching of dashboard queries.
  • Alerting: evaluators on streaming data with dedupe, routing to notification channels.
  • Deep dives: high cardinality, late data, multi tenant isolation, the monitoring of the monitoring system.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 2 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Hello Interview: Meta E5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/meta/e5)
Hello Interview: Google L5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/google/l5)

fields.Question: A crawler must remember billions of seen URLs in memory. Occasionally skipping a new URL is acceptable. Which structure?
fields.Choices:
A Bloom filter
A hash set of full URLs
A database lookup per URL
HyperLogLog
fields.Correct: A Bloom filter
fields.Explanation: A Bloom filter answers "seen?" in a few bits per URL with a tunable false positive rate, which here means rarely skipping a new page. A hash set of full URLs needs hundreds of GB. A database lookup per URL is slow at crawl rates. HyperLogLog estimates how many distinct URLs, not whether a given one was seen.
fields.Source:
Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/362686.362692)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Your crawler hammers some sites with hundreds of requests per second and gets blocked. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
A single global FIFO frontier
More crawler threads
Rotating IP addresses
Per host queues with a delay between requests, and obey robots.txt
fields.Correct: Per host queues with a delay between requests, and obey robots.txt
fields.Explanation: Mapping each host to one queue with a minimum delay bounds the load per site, and robots.txt states the site's rules. A global FIFO keeps sending bursts of the same host's links. More threads hit sites harder. Rotating IPs to evade blocks is abuse, not politeness.
fields.Source:
Mercator: A Scalable, Extensible Web Crawler (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1019213109274)
RFC 9309: Robots Exclusion Protocol (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9309)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Many different URLs return identical pages (tracking parameters, mirrors). How do you avoid storing and parsing them repeatedly?
fields.Choices:
Dedupe only on exact URL strings
Compare each page byte by byte with every stored page
Store a content fingerprint (checksum or simhash) and skip pages already seen
Ignore it, storage is cheap
fields.Correct: Store a content fingerprint (checksum or simhash) and skip pages already seen
fields.Explanation: Fingerprints catch duplicate content under different URLs in one lookup, and simhash also catches near duplicates. URL dedupe misses different URLs with the same content. Byte comparison with every page is quadratic. Duplicates waste crawl budget and fetch capacity, not just storage.
fields.Source:
Mercator: A Scalable, Extensible Web Crawler (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1019213109274)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Design a web crawler for a billion pages a month.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: polite, scalable, robust to traps and bad HTML, freshness.
  • Estimates: 1B per month is about 400 pages per second, times page size for bandwidth and storage.
  • Components: URL frontier (prioritized, per host queues), DNS cache, fetchers, parser, URL filter and seen set (Bloom filter), content dedupe, blob store.
  • Deep dives: politeness and robots.txt, crawler traps (depth limits), distributing the frontier by host hash, recrawl scheduling.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
The System Design Primer (https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer)
Mercator: A Scalable, Extensible Web Crawler (https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1019213109274)

fields.Question: Search autocomplete at 100k QPS must return the top 5 suggestions for a prefix in under 50 ms. Which approach?
fields.Choices:
A trie with the top 5 completions precomputed at each prefix node
SQL LIKE 'prefix%' with ORDER BY count on every keystroke
Walk the trie subtree and sort all completions per request
Full text search of all queries per keystroke
fields.Correct: A trie with the top 5 completions precomputed at each prefix node
fields.Explanation: Precomputing top K per node makes each lookup O(prefix length), and the trie is rebuilt offline from query logs. LIKE with ordering at 100k QPS is far too slow. Walking a short prefix's subtree touches millions of nodes. Full text search answers a different question and is slower.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A job scheduler: a job must not run twice concurrently, even if a worker dies mid run. What do you use?
fields.Choices:
A lock with no expiry
A lock with a TTL but no fencing
Delete the job from the queue before running it
A lease with heartbeat renewal and a fencing token, plus idempotent job steps
fields.Correct: A lease with heartbeat renewal and a fencing token, plus idempotent job steps
fields.Explanation: A lease expires if the worker dies so another can take over, the fencing token stops a paused old worker from writing, and idempotent steps make the rare retry safe. A lock with no expiry is stuck forever after a crash. TTL without fencing lets a zombie worker write after its lease ended. Deleting first loses the job if the worker crashes.
fields.Hint: Expire, fence, and make it safe to repeat.
fields.Source:
How to do distributed locking (https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html)
Hello Interview: OpenAI L5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/openai/l5)

fields.Question: Twenty worker processes poll a PostgreSQL jobs table for rows with run_at at or before now. They keep blocking on and double claiming the same rows. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Every worker reads all due jobs and runs them
Run a single scheduler process with no failover
Claim rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction that marks them running
Have each worker sleep a random time before polling
fields.Correct: Claim rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside a transaction that marks them running
fields.Explanation: SKIP LOCKED lets each worker lock a different set of due rows without waiting, which is the standard queue on Postgres pattern. Everyone running all due jobs is the double run bug. A single process is a single point of failure. Random sleeps reduce collisions but do not prevent them.
fields.Hint: Lock rows others are not using.
fields.Source: PostgreSQL: SELECT, The Locking Clause (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html)

fields.Question: Design a CI system like GitHub Actions for many organizations. Requirements, scheduling and isolation.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: trigger on push, run DAGs of jobs, stream logs, cache artifacts, fair across orgs, isolate untrusted code.
  • Flow: webhook to event store, workflow parser builds a DAG, ready jobs to per org queues, scheduler assigns runners.
  • Runners: ephemeral VMs or containers, leases with heartbeats, retry on lost runner.
  • Fairness: per org concurrency quotas, weighted fair scheduling, priority for interactive runs.
  • Deep dives: log streaming, artifact and dependency cache, autoscaling the runner pool, secrets handling.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: OpenAI L5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/openai/l5)
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)

fields.Question: A sync client has a 1 GB file synced. The user changes a few bytes. How do you avoid uploading the whole file again?
fields.Choices:
Split files into hashed chunks and upload only chunks whose hash is new
Upload the whole file and diff on the server
Compress the file before uploading again
Upload a byte level diff against the previous version only
fields.Correct: Split files into hashed chunks and upload only chunks whose hash is new
fields.Explanation: Content addressed chunks mean only changed chunks travel and identical chunks across users dedupe for free, as Dropbox does. Uploading then diffing still sends 1 GB. Compression shrinks but still resends everything. A byte diff against one previous version gives no dedupe and breaks if versions diverge.
fields.Source:
Rewriting the heart of our sync engine (https://dropbox.tech/infrastructure/rewriting-the-heart-of-our-sync-engine)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Where do you keep file bytes and file metadata (names, folders, versions, sharing) in a Drive like service?
fields.Choices:
Both in the relational database as BLOB columns
Both in the object store as JSON sidecar files
Bytes on each app server's local disk
Bytes in an object store, metadata in a database
fields.Correct: Bytes in an object store, metadata in a database
fields.Explanation: Object stores are cheap and durable for large blobs; metadata needs transactions and queries (move folder, list, share). BLOBs in the database bloat it and slow backups. JSON sidecars cannot do atomic renames or queries. Local disks are lost with the server and not shared.
fields.Source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: Mobile users upload 2 GB videos over flaky connections. Uploads keep failing at 80%. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
A single PUT through the app server with a longer timeout
Ask users to use Wi-Fi
Multipart upload with presigned URLs straight to object storage, retrying only failed parts
Base64 encode the file in a JSON request
fields.Correct: Multipart upload with presigned URLs straight to object storage, retrying only failed parts
fields.Explanation: Multipart splits the file into parts that upload and retry independently, and presigned URLs keep the bytes off your servers. A single PUT restarts from zero on any drop. Asking for Wi-Fi is not a design. Base64 adds a third to the size and is still one request.
fields.Source: Amazon S3: Uploading and copying objects using multipart upload (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html)

fields.Question: Design Dropbox or Google Drive file sync.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: upload, download, sync across devices, sharing, versions, large files.
  • Storage: chunked content addressed blobs in an object store, metadata DB (files, versions, chunk lists, ACLs).
  • Upload: client chunks and hashes, asks which chunks are missing, uploads them via presigned URLs, commits a new version.
  • Sync: change log with cursors per device, notify via long poll or WebSocket.
  • Deep dives: conflict handling (conflicted copy), dedupe, large folder moves, consistency of the metadata DB.
fields.Source:
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)
Rewriting the heart of our sync engine (https://dropbox.tech/infrastructure/rewriting-the-heart-of-our-sync-engine)
Hello Interview: Meta E5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/meta/e5)

fields.Question: Viewers watch on mobile networks whose bandwidth swings every few seconds. How do you deliver smooth playback?
fields.Choices:
Transcode several bitrates, cut into short segments, and let the player switch per segment (HLS or DASH)
Stream one high bitrate MP4 file
Detect bandwidth once on the server at start
Send raw uploads and let the client transcode
fields.Correct: Transcode several bitrates, cut into short segments, and let the player switch per segment (HLS or DASH)
fields.Explanation: Adaptive bitrate streaming lets the player pick the next segment's quality as bandwidth changes. One high bitrate file stalls on slow networks. A single measurement at start goes stale. Raw uploads are huge and phones cannot transcode them live.
fields.Hint: Let the player choose per segment.
fields.Source:
RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8216)
System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide, Volume 1 (https://blog.bytebytego.com/p/system-design-interview-books-volume)

fields.Question: A small share of titles produces most video traffic, and demand is predictable each evening. How do you serve it cheaply?
fields.Choices:
Serve every stream from the origin data center
Add more origin servers in one region
Cache videos in the API servers
Pre-position popular titles on CDN or ISP edge caches during off peak hours
fields.Correct: Pre-position popular titles on CDN or ISP edge caches during off peak hours
fields.Explanation: Netflix Open Connect fills edge appliances off peak so evening traffic is served near viewers. Origin serving pays full backbone cost and latency. More origin servers in one region do not fix distance. API servers are not built to serve video bytes.
fields.Source: Netflix Open Connect (https://openconnect.netflix.com/en/)

fields.Question: A collaborative editor must let users edit offline for days and merge peer to peer with no central server. Which approach fits?
fields.Choices:
Operational transformation with a central server
Last write wins on the whole document
CRDTs
Lock each paragraph while someone edits
fields.Correct: CRDTs
fields.Explanation: CRDTs converge without a central ordering, which suits offline and peer to peer. OT (as in Google Docs) relies on a server to order operations, which the constraints exclude. Last write wins discards one user's work. Locks do not work offline.
fields.Source: Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (https://inria.hal.science/inria-00609399)

fields.Question: Design Google Docs collaborative editing.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: concurrent editing with low latency, cursors and presence, history, offline edits.
  • Sync: WebSocket per document to a session server that owns the document.
  • Concurrency: OT with the server ordering operations, or CRDTs; explain the tradeoff (server dependency vs metadata overhead).
  • Storage: operation log plus periodic snapshots.
  • Deep dives: routing all editors of a doc to one server, scaling hot documents, reconnect and replay, permissions.
fields.Hint: Owner per doc, OT or CRDT.
fields.Source:
Hello Interview: Amazon L6 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/amazon/l6)
Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (https://inria.hal.science/inria-00609399)

fields.Question: An inference service wraps one GPU that processes batches of up to 100 prompts. Callers are synchronous. How do you batch?
fields.Choices:
Queue requests and dispatch when the batch hits 100 or a max wait such as 20 ms passes
Always wait until 100 requests arrive
Send each request to the GPU on its own
Batch by caller and wait for each caller's next request
fields.Correct: Queue requests and dispatch when the batch hits 100 or a max wait such as 20 ms passes
fields.Explanation: Max size plus max wait trades a small bounded delay for throughput, and each response is routed back by request id. Waiting for 100 makes latency unbounded at low traffic. One request per call wastes most of the GPU. Waiting on a caller's next request does not apply to synchronous callers.
fields.Source: Anthropic system design interview (https://www.aced.io/blog/anthropic-system-design-interview)

fields.Question: LLM requests produce between 10 and 4,000 output tokens. With static batches, short requests wait for the longest one in their batch. What fixes it?
fields.Choices:
Use a larger static batch size
Sort requests by arrival time
Give each request its own GPU
Continuous (iteration level) batching: add and remove requests from the batch at each decoding step
fields.Correct: Continuous (iteration level) batching: add and remove requests from the batch at each decoding step
fields.Explanation: Scheduling per decoding step lets finished sequences leave and new ones join, as in Orca and later vLLM style servers, so short requests are not held hostage. Larger static batches make the waiting worse. Arrival order does not change who waits. A GPU per request wastes most of the hardware.
fields.Hint: Schedule per token, not per batch.
fields.Source: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models (https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu)

fields.Question: An LLM API serves many customers whose requests vary 100x in token count. How do you rate limit fairly by cost?
fields.Choices:
Requests per minute per tenant
One global queue in arrival order
Per tenant limits on tokens per minute, estimated at admission and corrected after completion
Buy bigger GPUs so limits are not needed
fields.Correct: Per tenant limits on tokens per minute, estimated at admission and corrected after completion
fields.Explanation: Tokens track GPU cost, so a token budget per tenant keeps a heavy tenant from crowding others. Request counts let one 4,000 token prompt cost the same as a 40 token one. A global queue lets one tenant starve others. Hardware does not remove contention.
fields.Source:
Fairness in multi-tenant systems (https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/fairness-in-multi-tenant-systems/)
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)

fields.Question: Design a chat completion service in front of a fleet of GPU model servers. Treat the model as a black box.
fields.Answer:
• Requirements: stream tokens, high GPU utilization, per tenant fairness, bounded latency, survive server loss.
  • API: POST /chat returning a token stream (SSE).
  • Gateway: auth, token based rate limits, admission control and load shedding.
  • Scheduling: per model queues, continuous batching on servers, route by load and cache affinity.
  • Failures: retries for requests that have not started streaming, health checks, capacity headroom.
  • Deep dives: queueing and backpressure, multi tenant fairness, conversation storage, cost tracking.
fields.Source:
Anthropic system design interview (https://www.aced.io/blog/anthropic-system-design-interview)
OpenAI system design interview (https://www.tryexponent.com/blog/openai-system-design-interview)
Hello Interview: OpenAI L5 interview guide (https://www.hellointerview.com/guides/openai/l5)
